name: Product demonstration language
controls: The rhetorical device a product video uses to explain what a feature does: how the demo is driven, structured, focused and sourced.
question: How should the video show what the product does?
notes: Demo devices combine: a typical launch film is a cursor-driven demo + input-to-output structure + zoomed detail on a recreated interface. Pick at most one per family as a starting point. 'Walkthrough', 'demo' and 'tour' are used loosely in the industry; here they are distinguished by who drives (viewer-proxy cursor, narrator, or the product itself). Source options (screen recording, recreated, fake) overlap with ui-treatment fidelity: ui-treatment says how the UI looks, product-demo says how the footage was made and used to argue. Narrative dimension governs the whole-film arc; product-demo governs how individual features are explained.

families.name: Focus (what the camera and edit emphasise)
Source (how the interface footage is made)

options.what: The product is shown being used step by step in real sequence, with nothing skipped or dramatised.
options.looks: Full screens in real order, real navigation, minimal cutting, captions or narration labelling each step.
options.motion: Real-time or lightly sped UI interactions, continuous camera, few edits.
options.use: Tutorials, onboarding, sales demos, help-center videos.
options.conveys: Transparency and learnability: this is exactly how it works.
options.vs: Guided walkthrough adds editorial emphasis (zooms, highlights, skipped steps); literal walkthrough shows everything as it happens.
options.prompt: Show the feature used in its true sequence from start to finish: every screen in order, real navigation, interactions at 1-1.5x real speed, a continuous frame with no dramatic camera moves; label each step with a short caption (4-7 words) in a consistent position.

options.what: A walkthrough edited and directed to steer attention: steps compressed, key moments zoomed and highlighted.
options.looks: Product sequence with camera push-ins, spotlight dimming, captions and callouts; trivial steps cut.
options.motion: Eased camera moves between regions of interest, time-compressed transitions, highlight pulses on the active control.
options.use: Feature launches, marketing demos, landing-page videos.
options.conveys: Clarity with pace; the viewer is led, not left to search.
options.vs: Literal walkthrough shows everything; guided walkthrough edits and emphasises. Cursor-driven demo is about the cursor as driver; guided walkthrough can be cursor-free.
options.prompt: Walk through the feature in order but direct attention: skip trivial steps with quick cuts or 3-5x time compression, push the camera 1.5-2x into each active region (800 ms power3.inOut), dim non-active UI to 40%, and add one caption per key step.

options.what: An animated cursor acts as the viewer's proxy, performing every interaction.
options.looks: Enlarged cursor moving across the UI, clicks with press states, hover responses, text typing into fields.
options.motion: Curved, eased cursor paths; 150-300 ms dwell before each click; UI responds within 60-120 ms; camera may follow the cursor.
options.use: Web and desktop product demos, launch films, landing heroes.
options.conveys: Ease of use: a person just did this in a few clicks.
options.vs: Hands-free automated demo has no cursor: the product acts on its own. Guided walkthrough may use a cursor but is defined by editorial emphasis.
options.prompt: Drive the demo with a single enlarged (1.5-2x) cursor as the viewer's proxy: curved eased paths of 500-900 ms, a 200 ms dwell before each click, a 0.9 dip on click, and the UI responding within 100 ms; keep the cursor in frame at all times and let the camera follow it gently.

options.what: The interface operates by itself with no visible cursor or hand: states change, data flows, results appear.
options.looks: Clean UI changing state autonomously; elements highlight, fill and animate as if powered by the product.
options.motion: State changes triggered by timing and choreography rather than input; staggered updates, morphs, and auto-scrolls.
options.use: Automation, AI and background-process products; hero loops; brand-led launch films.
options.conveys: Automation and magic: it works without you.
options.vs: Cursor-driven demo shows a human operating; hands-free implies the product itself is doing the work.
options.prompt: Show no cursor or touch indicators: let the interface change state on its own in a choreographed sequence (fields fill, cards update, charts redraw, rows reorder) with 60-120 ms staggers and eased morphs, so the product appears to act autonomously.

options.what: A human presenter on camera or in a picture-in-picture bubble narrates while the product is shown.
options.looks: Presenter footage alternating with or overlaid on UI (circular or rounded-rectangle PiP in a corner), lower-third name label.
options.motion: Cuts or wipes between presenter and UI; PiP scales and repositions to avoid covering the action.
options.use: Founder launch videos, keynotes, sales demos, YouTube product content.
options.conveys: Trust and personality: a real person stands behind this.
options.vs: Guided walkthrough relies on graphics for direction; presenter-led relies on a human voice and face. Narrative dimension defines the talk structure.
options.prompt: Combine presenter footage with the product: place the presenter in a 240-320px circular or 16px-radius picture-in-picture in a lower corner with a subtle border and shadow, move it with 400 ms eases to avoid the active UI, and cut to full-frame presenter only for key statements.

options.what: Show what goes in, then what comes out, making the product the transformation between them.
options.looks: An input (prompt, file, data) clearly presented, a brief process beat, then the output presented larger or richer.
options.motion: Input enters and is submitted; a short processing moment (under 1.5 s); output resolves with emphasis; often side by side at the end.
options.use: AI products, converters, generators, APIs, automation.
options.conveys: Capability and leverage: small input, big result.
options.vs: Before/after compares two states of the same thing; input-output shows a transformation of one thing into another.
options.prompt: Structure each beat as input then output: present the input clearly (e.g. a prompt typed into a field, a file dropped in), hold it 800 ms, show a processing beat under 1.5 s, then reveal the output at a larger scale with a 1-1.5 s hold; end with input and output side by side if space allows.

options.what: Dramatise a pain point first, then show the product resolving it.
options.looks: Problem beat in muted or chaotic visuals (clutter, errors, red states, many tabs), solution beat in clean, bright product UI.
options.motion: Problem uses jittery, cluttered, overlapping motion or slowness; solution uses calm, confident, orderly motion.
options.use: Launch films, ads, sales videos, explainers.
options.conveys: Relief and relevance: this solves your problem.
options.vs: Before/after shows two states; problem-solution tells a causal story with tension and resolution. Narrative dimension may use it for the whole film; here it explains one feature.
options.prompt: Open with a 2-4 s problem beat in desaturated or cluttered visuals (overlapping windows, error states, repeated manual steps, faster jittery motion), then cut to the product solving it with clean, saturated UI and calm eased motion; make the contrast in color, density and pace obvious.

options.what: Show the same thing in two states, before and after the product acts, to make the change undeniable.
options.looks: Two states of one object (document, image, dashboard, code) either sequential or with a split wipe divider.
options.motion: Wipe slider moving across the frame, crossfade or morph between states, toggle flip that switches the whole frame.
options.use: Editing tools, design and photo products, optimisation tools, redesigns.
options.conveys: Measurable improvement.
options.vs: Side-by-side shows both simultaneously for comparison; before/after is typically a transition from one to the other. Input-output transforms different things.
options.prompt: Show the same object in its before state for 1-1.5 s, then reveal the after state with a vertical wipe divider (2px line with a round handle) travelling left to right over 1-1.4 s power2.inOut; label each side with small 'Before' and 'After' chips, and optionally drag the divider back halfway to compare.

options.what: Two alternatives shown simultaneously in split frames for direct comparison.
options.looks: Frame split vertically or horizontally, each half labeled (old way vs new way, competitor vs us, manual vs automated), often with a timer.
options.motion: Both sides play simultaneously; the product's side finishes first; a timer or counter emphasises the difference.
options.use: Speed claims, competitor comparisons, old-vs-new workflows.
options.conveys: Objective superiority.
options.vs: Before/after sequences states of one thing; side-by-side runs alternatives in parallel. Race comparisons are a common side-by-side variant.
search: side by side speed test animation
options.prompt: Split the frame into two equal halves with a 2px divider; label each (e.g. 'Manual' and 'With [product]') at the top; play both processes simultaneously with visible timers; let the product side finish much sooner, then dim the other side to 40% and scale the winning side up slightly.

options.what: A feature explained as a small number of numbered, discrete steps.
options.looks: Large step numbers or a stepper indicator (1, 2, 3), one UI moment per step, short labels.
options.motion: Step indicator advances; each step's UI moment plays then transitions to the next with consistent rhythm.
options.use: Onboarding, how-it-works sections, tutorials, landing pages.
options.conveys: Simplicity: it only takes three steps.
options.vs: Literal walkthrough shows every action; step-by-step groups them into a few labelled chunks. Workflow visualization shows the system, not user steps.
options.prompt: Break the feature into 3-4 numbered steps; show a persistent stepper (1, 2, 3) whose active number fills with accent; give each step one UI moment of 2-3 s with a short label, and transition between steps with a consistent 500 ms horizontal slide so the rhythm is regular.

options.what: The flow of data or work through a system shown as connected nodes and paths.
options.looks: Nodes (apps, steps, services) connected by lines; packets, pulses or cards travelling along the connections.
options.motion: Connectors draw on, pulses travel node to node, nodes activate in sequence, branches split and merge.
options.use: Automation, integrations, infrastructure, AI agent pipelines.
options.conveys: System clarity and orchestration.
options.vs: User journey follows a person; workflow visualization follows data or tasks. Step-by-step is user steps; canvas UI (ui-treatment) is when the product itself is a node editor.
options.prompt: Represent the workflow as 4-7 nodes (rounded cards with app icons and labels) connected by 1.5-2px paths; draw connectors on with stroke-dashoffset (400 ms each), then send glowing pulses along them in sequence; activate each node (accent border, subtle scale 1.04) when a pulse arrives.

options.what: The product shown through a person's path across moments, contexts and touchpoints.
options.looks: A sequence of moments (discovery, first use, success) often with persona avatars, devices and contexts; path line connecting them.
options.motion: Travel along a path or timeline, scene-to-scene transitions tied to the person's progress, device switches.
options.use: Consumer products, cross-device products, platform stories, sales narratives.
options.conveys: Empathy and relevance in real life.
options.vs: Workflow visualization follows data through a system; user journey follows a person through time. Use-case vignette shows one situation, not a full path.
options.prompt: Follow one persona through 3-5 moments: introduce them with an avatar and name label, then show each moment as a scene with the relevant UI, connected by a path line or timeline that advances between scenes; keep the persona visible or referenced in every scene.

options.what: A short, concrete situation showing one type of user getting value from the product.
options.looks: Real-looking content specific to a role (a designer's file, a marketer's campaign, a developer's repo) inside the UI, often labeled with the role.
options.motion: Compact demo loop of 4-8 s per vignette; vignettes often chained with quick transitions.
options.use: Multi-audience products, landing pages with role tabs, sales enablement.
options.conveys: It's for people like me.
options.vs: User journey spans many moments for one person; a vignette is one moment, often several vignettes for several roles. Feature montage cuts between features, not users.
options.prompt: Show 2-4 short vignettes of 4-8 s each, each labeled with a role chip (e.g. 'Design', 'Engineering', 'Marketing'); fill the UI with content specific to that role and show one clear outcome per vignette; transition between them with a consistent quick slide or tab switch.

options.what: Content or actions passing between the product and other apps or devices.
options.looks: Several app windows or device screens; an object (message, file, card) visibly travels from one to another; app icons as anchors.
options.motion: An element lifts out of one interface, travels on an arc and lands in another, which reacts.
options.use: Integrations, platform ecosystems, cross-device continuity features.
options.conveys: Connectedness: it works with everything you use.
options.vs: Workflow visualization abstracts apps into nodes; cross-app flow shows the real interfaces and the object moving between them.
options.prompt: Show 2-3 app windows or device screens; lift an element out of the first (scale 1.05, shadow grows), fly it on a curved arc to the second over 700-900 ms power2.inOut, and have the destination react on landing (highlight, new row inserted, notification).

options.what: One feature is shown alone, separated from the rest of the product, so nothing competes.
options.looks: The relevant component or panel extracted onto a clean background or with the rest of the UI removed or heavily dimmed.
options.motion: The component lifts out of the full UI (or the UI fades away around it), then its interaction plays in isolation.
options.use: Feature reveals, social cut-downs, changelog clips.
options.conveys: Focus: this one thing matters.
options.vs: Zoomed detail magnifies within context; feature isolation removes the context. Abstracted UI (ui-treatment) is the visual result of isolation.
options.prompt: Isolate one feature: fade the surrounding interface to 0 (or 20%) over 400 ms while the relevant component lifts slightly (scale 1.05-1.2, shadow grows) and recenters on a clean background; play its interaction alone, then optionally return it to the full UI.

options.what: Many features shown in rapid succession, each for a second or two, to convey breadth.
options.looks: Quick cuts between different UI moments, each with a one- or two-word label; consistent framing or match cuts.
options.motion: Fast rhythm, cuts on the beat (0.8-2 s per feature), match cuts or whip transitions, labels snapping in.
options.use: Launch film finales, sizzle reels, release recaps, ads.
options.conveys: Breadth, power, momentum.
options.vs: Feature isolation goes deep on one; montage goes wide across many. Pacing dimension sets the edit rhythm.
options.prompt: Cut through 6-12 features at 0.8-1.6 s each, on the music beat; keep framing consistent (same scale and position) so cuts read as a rhythm; snap a 1-3 word label in for each (100 ms) and use match cuts where one feature's shape leads into the next.

options.what: The camera magnifies a small region of the UI to show a detail that would be invisible at full view.
options.looks: Full UI, then a push-in to a region at 2-4x; or a magnifier loupe circle over the detail.
options.motion: Smooth camera push (800-1200 ms power3.inOut) to the region, hold for the interaction, pull back; or a loupe that scales in over the spot.
options.use: Micro-interactions, small but important features, polish details.
options.conveys: Craft and attention to detail.
options.vs: Feature isolation removes context; zoomed detail keeps it and magnifies. Zoom in ui-interaction is in-product zoom; this is an editorial camera move.
options.prompt: Push the camera into a small UI region at 2.5-3x over 1 s power3.inOut, keeping the detail centered and rendered sharply at final resolution; hold 1.5-2.5 s while the interaction plays; pull back to the full view with the same curve. Alternative: scale in a 240-320px circular loupe with a 2px border over the detail.

options.what: Editorial graphics layered over the UI (labels, leader lines, circles, arrows) to name and explain parts.
options.looks: Short labels connected by thin leader lines to UI elements, highlight rings, arrows, numbered markers; styled distinct from the product UI.
options.motion: Leader lines draw from the element to the label (200-300 ms), labels fade and slide 6-8px, rings scale in around targets.
options.use: Explainers, feature tours, technical products, tutorials.
options.conveys: Clarity and instruction.
options.vs: Tooltips are part of the product; callout annotations are a layer added by the video. Blueprint UI annotates construction; callouts annotate meaning.
options.prompt: Annotate the UI with an overlay layer styled differently from the product: 1.5px leader lines drawing from a 6px dot on the element to a label (200-300 ms), labels in 16-20px medium weight with a subtle pill background sliding 6px into place, and highlight rings scaling from 0.8 to 1 around targets; show no more than 3 callouts at once.

options.what: A feature explained through a visual metaphor rather than the interface (a funnel for filtering, a shield for security).
options.looks: Symbolic objects, illustrations or 3D forms standing for the feature, often with minimal or no UI.
options.motion: The metaphor acts out the function: items fall through a filter, a shield blocks particles, threads weave together.
options.use: Brand films, explainers for invisible features (security, performance, infrastructure).
options.conveys: Understanding of an abstract benefit.
options.vs: UI to abstract visualization starts from the real UI and transforms; conceptual metaphor may never show UI. Metaphorical/faux UI (ui-treatment) uses UI grammar as the metaphor.
options.prompt: Explain the feature with one clear visual metaphor instead of UI (e.g. a funnel sorting particles for filtering, a shield deflecting shapes for security); keep the metaphor simple (1-3 objects), animate it performing the function, and anchor it with a short label naming the actual feature.

options.what: Real interface elements transform into an abstract visualization of what they mean or do.
options.looks: UI components morph into shapes, particles, lines or diagrams (list rows become bars, cards become nodes).
options.motion: Morph transitions: elements lose UI detail, change shape and flow into the abstract system.
options.use: Explaining what happens behind the interface, AI and data products, launch film transitions.
options.conveys: Depth beneath the surface; the product's inner logic.
options.vs: Abstract to UI goes the other way (idea resolves into product). Exploded UI separates layers but stays UI.
options.prompt: Start with the real UI, then morph its elements into abstract forms over 1-1.5 s: strip text and icons first (fade 200 ms), then interpolate shapes (rows into bars, cards into nodes, dots into particles) and flow them into an abstract diagram representing the underlying process.

options.what: An abstract form or idea resolves into the real product interface.
options.looks: Shapes, particles or lines coalesce and snap into cards, rows and controls of the actual UI.
options.motion: Converging motion: scattered elements travel, align to the grid and gain UI detail (text, icons fade in last).
options.use: Launch film openers, brand-to-product transitions, feature reveals.
options.conveys: The idea made real.
options.vs: UI to abstract explains what's behind the product; abstract to UI reveals the product as the embodiment of an idea.
options.prompt: Begin with abstract forms (particles, lines, colored shapes) in motion, then converge them over 1-1.5 s onto the UI grid: shapes interpolate into card and row rectangles, snap into alignment, and finally fade in text and icons (200 ms, 30 ms stagger) to reveal the real interface.

options.what: An action in the interface cuts or morphs to its outcome in the physical world.
options.looks: UI action (tap 'Order', 'Send', 'Print') followed by footage or 3D of the real result (package arriving, lights turning on, a printed object).
options.motion: Match cut or morph from a UI element to a real object with the same shape or position; camera continuity across the transition.
options.use: Commerce, logistics, IoT and hardware, fintech, consumer apps.
options.conveys: Tangible impact; software that changes real things.
options.vs: Conceptual metaphor symbolises; UI to real-world shows the literal outcome. In-context UI (ui-treatment) puts UI in a real scene; this cuts from UI to the world.
search: UI to real world match cut
app action real world result video
options.prompt: End the UI action on a clear shape (e.g. the tapped button or a map pin), then match-cut or morph that shape into the real-world result (footage or 3D) in the same frame position within 300-500 ms, keeping camera direction continuous across the cut.

options.what: The interface is pulled apart into its layers to explain how it is built or how parts relate.
options.looks: The screen separated into stacked layers in 3D, each labeled (data, logic, components, presentation).
options.motion: Layers separate in z while the camera orbits, labels draw on per layer, then layers recompose.
options.use: Platform and architecture explainers, design systems, technical launches.
options.conveys: Depth, engineering rigor, how it works under the hood.
options.vs: Exploded UI (ui-treatment) is the visual construction; exploded-interface explanation is using it to argue, with labels and a narrative about the layers.
options.prompt: Separate the screen into 3-5 layers along z (100-200px gaps) while rotating the stack to 50 degrees X and -30 degrees Z over 1.4 s power3.inOut; draw a leader-line label for each layer naming its role, hold 2 s, then collapse the layers back into the flat screen.

options.what: Long real processes shown at accelerated speed, with a visible time indicator, to prove what is possible.
options.looks: UI changing rapidly with a clock, timer or '10x' badge in the corner; content building up quickly.
options.motion: Speed ramps: normal speed for the key moment, accelerate through repetition, slow down for the result.
options.use: Showing end-to-end builds, long AI or automation runs, creative tools making something complex.
options.conveys: Scale of accomplishment and honesty about duration.
options.vs: Side-by-side races compare two processes; time-compressed shows one process sped up. Pacing dimension sets overall edit speed.
options.prompt: Play the start of the process at real speed for 1-2 s, ramp to 8-20x speed through repetitive work (ease the speed change over 300 ms), show a timer or speed badge in a corner, then ramp back to real speed for the final result and hold it 1.5 s.

options.what: A short seamless loop demonstrating one feature, designed for landing pages and social autoplay.
options.looks: One compact demo moment framed tightly, no intro or outro, final state matching the first frame.
options.motion: 4-10 s cycle; the end state resets invisibly (content clears, cursor returns) to the start state.
options.use: Landing-page heroes, feature sections, social posts, docs.
options.conveys: Instant comprehension without sound or context.
options.vs: Feature isolation is a focus choice; looping hero demo is a format constraint (seamless, silent, short) that can use any driver.
options.prompt: Build a 4-10 s seamless loop around one feature: no titles, readable without sound, the final frame identical to the first; reset state invisibly (fade content out over 300 ms and return the cursor on an eased path) so the loop point is undetectable.

options.what: Real screen capture of the product, polished in post with zooms, cursor smoothing, backgrounds and callouts.
options.looks: The real app (real data, real timing) placed on a styled background with rounded corners and shadow; automatic zooms following clicks; smoothed, enlarged cursor.
options.motion: Auto-zoom push-ins on clicks (1.5-2x), smoothed cursor paths, speed-ups over dead time, motion blur on zoom.
options.use: Fast-turnaround demos, changelogs, tutorials, founder videos, social.
options.conveys: Authenticity with polish; this is the real product.
options.vs: Recreated interface rebuilds the UI as vectors or HTML for full control; screen recording keeps real pixels and real behavior. Production-faithful UI is the recreated equivalent.
options.prompt: Place the real screen recording on a styled background (gradient or solid) with 12-16px rounded corners and a soft shadow at 85-90% of frame; auto-zoom 1.5-2x toward each click over 600-800 ms power3.inOut; smooth and enlarge the cursor; speed up idle stretches 4-8x; add a brief highlight ring on each click.

options.what: The product UI rebuilt from design files or code as animatable layers, faithful to the real product.
options.looks: Crisp vector-clean UI that matches the product, at any resolution, with clean data and no jank.
options.motion: Any motion is possible: layers animate independently, camera moves freely, states are choreographed precisely.
options.use: Launch films, marketing sites, keynote videos, anywhere polish matters.
options.conveys: Premium polish while staying truthful.
options.vs: Screen recording is real pixels; recreated interface is real design rebuilt. Fake/stylized interface does not match the real product.
search: Figma to motion UI launch film
options.prompt: Rebuild the interface from the product's design system as separate animatable layers (HTML/CSS or vectors): match layout, type, colors and components to the real product, use clean representative data, and animate every element independently for choreographed state changes.

options.what: An invented interface that suggests the product without representing its real screens.
options.looks: Plausible but idealised UI: simplified or invented layouts, perfect data, brand-heavy styling.
options.motion: Free, expressive motion unconstrained by real behavior.
options.use: Pre-launch products, brand films, concept pitches, ads where real UI is too complex.
options.conveys: Vision and feeling over specifics. Risk: can mislead if presented as the real product.
options.vs: Recreated interface matches the real product; fake/stylized does not. Stylized UI (ui-treatment) is the look; this is the sourcing decision.
options.prompt: Design an invented interface that expresses the product's idea: plausible components, idealised data, brand colors and type, and only the elements that carry the message; do not imply exact real screens, and keep it internally consistent across shots.
